challenges.title: Base64 Decoding
challenges.brief: An API token that is Base64-encoded (twice). No key needed - decode it to read the data.
challenges.hint:
This is Base64, not encryption. Decode it... then notice the result is
STILL Base64, so decode again.  CyberChef: 'From Base64' (x2), or the terminal.
challenges.scenario: During a web-application assessment you intercept an API request whose body is an opaque-looking string. It is not encrypted - it is Base64-encoded, and in fact encoded twice. Because Base64 has no key, you can simply decode it and read the data it carries.
challenges.objective: Decode the Base64 token (it is double-encoded) and read the flag inside.

steps.title: Inspect the token
steps.desc: It uses only A-Z a-z 0-9 + / with '=' padding - the classic Base64 alphabet.

steps.title: Decode the first Base64 layer
steps.desc: The output will still look like Base64 - that is expected, it was encoded twice.

steps.title: Decode the second layer
steps.desc: Pipe the first decode into base64 again to reach the plaintext and the SIS{...} flag.

steps.title: CyberChef alternative
steps.desc: Drop the token in and chain 'From Base64' twice, or use the 'Magic' operation to auto-detect.

challenges.title: Hex Decoding
challenges.brief: A value stored as a hexadecimal string. Convert it straight back to readable text.
challenges.hint:
This is hexadecimal (0-9, a-f). Convert it back to text.
CyberChef: 'From Hex'.  Terminal: pipe it through xxd -r -p.
challenges.scenario: A configuration file stores a value as a long hexadecimal string. Hex is an encoding (each byte written as two characters 0-9 a-f), not a cipher, so it converts straight back to readable text.
challenges.objective: Convert the hex string back to ASCII and read the flag.

steps.title: Look at the value
steps.desc: Only characters 0-9 and a-f, an even number of them - that is hexadecimal.

steps.title: Convert hex to text
steps.desc: xxd -r -p reverses a plain hex dump back to raw bytes.

steps.title: CyberChef alternative
steps.desc: Use the 'From Hex' operation to get the same result in the browser.

challenges.title: Binary Decoding
challenges.brief: A raw bit-stream where every 8 bits is one ASCII character. Convert binary back to text.
challenges.hint:
Every 8-bit group is one ASCII character. Convert binary -> text.
CyberChef: 'From Binary'.  Or a couple of lines of Python.
challenges.scenario: A device log records one of its fields as a raw bit-stream. Each group of eight bits is one ASCII character, so the stream converts directly back to text.
challenges.objective: Convert the 8-bit binary groups back to ASCII and read the flag.

steps.title: Inspect the stream
steps.desc: Space-separated groups of eight 1s and 0s - one byte each.

steps.title: Convert binary to text
steps.desc: Turn every 8-bit group into its character.

steps.title: CyberChef alternative
steps.desc: Use 'From Binary' (delimiter: Space) to decode it in the browser.

challenges.title: Caesar Cipher
challenges.brief: A note shifted with a Caesar cipher. Only 25 keys exist - brute-force them all.
challenges.hint:
A Caesar cipher has only 25 keys - try every shift.
CyberChef: 'ROT13 Brute Force'.  Or brute-force in one line of Python.
challenges.scenario: An old in-house application 'protects' a note with a Caesar cipher - every letter shifted by a fixed amount. With only 25 possible shifts, brute force recovers the note in seconds. This is why classical ciphers were abandoned for real algorithms.
challenges.objective: Brute-force the Caesar shift and read the flag inside the recovered message.

steps.title: Read the ciphertext
steps.desc: Readable letters, just shifted by an unknown fixed amount.

steps.title: Try all 25 shifts
steps.desc: One of the 25 lines will turn into plain English ending in a SIS{...} flag.
steps.cmd:
python3 - <<'EOF'
s=open('ciphertext.txt').read()
for k in range(1,26):
    print(k, ''.join(chr((ord(c)-65-k)%26+65) if c.isupper() else chr((ord(c)-97-k)%26+97) if c.islower() else c for c in s))
EOF

steps.title: CyberChef alternative
steps.desc: Use 'ROT13 Brute Force' and read the line that becomes English.

challenges.title: Atbash Cipher
challenges.brief: A message hidden with Atbash (the alphabet reversed). Apply it again to decode.
challenges.hint:
This is the Atbash cipher: the alphabet reversed (A<->Z, B<->Y ...).
Atbash is its own inverse - apply it again to decode.
CyberChef: 'Atbash Cipher'.
challenges.scenario: A message was obfuscated with the Atbash cipher, which replaces each letter with its mirror in the alphabet (A becomes Z, B becomes Y). Atbash is its own inverse, so applying it a second time reveals the text.
challenges.objective: Undo the Atbash substitution and read the flag.

steps.title: Read the ciphertext
steps.desc: A monoalphabetic substitution - each letter mapped to its alphabet mirror.

steps.title: Apply Atbash again to decode
steps.desc: Mirroring the alphabet a second time restores the original text.
steps.cmd: python3 -c "print(''.join(chr(219-ord(c)) if 'a'<=c<='z' else chr(155-ord(c)) if 'A'<=c<='Z' else c for c in open('ciphertext.txt').read()))"

steps.title: CyberChef alternative
steps.desc: Use the 'Atbash Cipher' operation.

challenges.title: Vigenere Cipher
challenges.brief: A Vigenere-encrypted message. You have the keyword - use it to decrypt.
challenges.hint:
This is a Vigenere cipher and you have the keyword (key.txt).
CyberChef: 'Vigenere Decode' and paste the key.  Or decrypt in Python.
challenges.scenario: A message was encrypted with the Vigenere cipher, which shifts each letter by a varying amount driven by a repeating keyword. During the assessment you already recovered the keyword, so decryption is straightforward.
challenges.objective: Use the recovered keyword to decrypt the Vigenere ciphertext and read the flag.

steps.title: Read the ciphertext and keyword
steps.desc: The keyword is in key.txt.

steps.title: Decrypt with the keyword
steps.desc: Subtract the keyword's letter shifts to recover the plaintext.

steps.title: CyberChef alternative
steps.desc: Use 'Vigenere Decode' and paste the keyword from key.txt.

challenges.title: AES-256-CBC Decrypt
challenges.brief: An AES-256-CBC file with the key and IV supplied. Decrypt it with OpenSSL.
challenges.hint:
AES-256 in CBC mode. You have the key and IV (key.txt).
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc  with  -K (key)  -iv (iv)  -in  -out
challenges.scenario: You recovered an AES-256-CBC encrypted file from a misconfigured backup, along with the key and initialisation vector that were stored next to it. With the key material in hand, OpenSSL decrypts it directly.
challenges.objective: Decrypt secret.enc with the supplied key and IV, then read the flag.

steps.title: Read the key and IV
steps.desc: key.txt holds a 64-hex-char AES-256 key and a 32-hex-char IV.

steps.title: Decrypt with OpenSSL
steps.desc: Pass the key to -K and the IV to -iv (both hex). Replace the placeholders with the real values.

steps.title: Read the flag
steps.desc: The decrypted file contains the SIS{...} flag.

challenges.title: RSA Decrypt (private key)
challenges.brief: A file encrypted for an RSA public key. You hold the private key - decrypt it.
challenges.hint:
message.enc was encrypted with an RSA public key. You hold the matching
PRIVATE key (private.pem) - use it to decrypt.
openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey private.pem -in message.enc
challenges.scenario: You obtained an RSA private key and a small file that was encrypted for the matching public key. Whatever the public key locked, only this private key can open - so the file decrypts cleanly.
challenges.objective: Use the RSA private key to decrypt message.enc and read the flag.

steps.title: Confirm what you have
steps.desc: private.pem is the RSA private key; message.enc is the ciphertext.

steps.title: Decrypt with the private key
steps.desc: pkeyutl -decrypt reverses the public-key encryption.

steps.title: Read the flag
steps.desc: The recovered plaintext carries the SIS{...} flag.

challenges.title: Hybrid Encryption (RSA + AES)
challenges.brief: An RSA-wrapped AES key plus an AES-encrypted blob - the TLS pattern. Unwrap, then decrypt.
challenges.hint:
Hybrid encryption (the TLS pattern):
 - session_key.enc = an AES key encrypted with RSA.
 - data.enc        = the data, encrypted with AES-256-CBC using that key.
1) RSA-decrypt session_key.enc with private.pem -> a 64-hex AES key.
2) AES-decrypt data.enc with that key (-K) and the IV in iv.txt.
challenges.scenario: A captured payload uses hybrid encryption - exactly how TLS works. A random AES session key was wrapped with RSA, and the bulk data was encrypted with that AES key. You hold the RSA private key, so you can unwrap the session key and then decrypt the data.
challenges.objective: RSA-decrypt the AES session key, then AES-decrypt the data blob to read the flag.

steps.title: Recover the AES session key with RSA
steps.desc: The result is a 64-hex-character AES key.
steps.cmd:
openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey private.pem -in session_key.enc -out sk.txt
cat sk.txt

steps.title: Read the IV
steps.desc: iv.txt holds the AES initialisation vector.

steps.title: Decrypt the data with AES
steps.desc: Feed the recovered key to -K and the IV to -iv.

challenges.title: Hash Crack - MD5
challenges.brief: An MD5 password hash from a database dump. Identify it and crack it with the wordlist.
challenges.hint:
Identify the hash, then crack it against wordlist.txt.
  hashid hash.txt
  hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt --show
  john --format=raw-md5 --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt
The cracked word goes inside the flag braces: SIS{crackedword}
challenges.scenario: You extracted a password hash from a leaked database dump during an authorised assessment. Hashes cannot be reversed, but weak passwords fall to a dictionary attack: hash every word in a list and compare. Identify the algorithm first, then crack it.
challenges.objective: Identify the hash type, crack it against the wordlist; the cracked password is the flag.

steps.title: Identify the hash
steps.desc: A 32-hex-character value is MD5.

steps.title: Crack it with the wordlist
steps.desc: Hashcat mode 0 is MD5. John works too if hashcat has no GPU.
steps.cmd:
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt --show
# or:
john --format=raw-md5 --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt

steps.title: Wrap the cracked word
steps.desc: Submit the recovered password as SIS{crackedword}.

challenges.title: Hash Crack - SHA-1
challenges.brief: A SHA-1 password hash. Confirm the type and crack it with the wordlist.
challenges.hint:
Identify the hash, then crack it against wordlist.txt.
  hashid hash.txt
  hashcat -m 100 -a 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt --show
  john --format=raw-sha1 --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt
The cracked word goes inside the flag braces: SIS{crackedword}
challenges.scenario: A second password hash turned up in the same dump, but it is a different algorithm. Confirm the type, then run the same style of dictionary attack against it.
challenges.objective: Identify the hash type, crack it against the wordlist; the cracked password is the flag.

steps.title: Identify the hash
steps.desc: A 40-hex-character value is SHA-1.

steps.title: Crack it with the wordlist
steps.desc: Hashcat mode 100 is SHA-1 (or use John).
steps.cmd:
hashcat -m 100 -a 0 hash.txt wordlist.txt --show
# or:
john --format=raw-sha1 --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt

steps.title: Wrap the cracked word
steps.desc: Submit the recovered password as SIS{crackedword}.

challenges.title: Integrity Check (SHA-256)
challenges.brief: An original file and a possibly tampered copy. Use SHA-256 to prove what changed.
challenges.hint:
One of the two files was tampered with. They look almost identical.
1) sha256sum original.txt tampered.txt  (the hashes differ)
2) diff them to see what changed (report it).
3) Prove you computed it: python3 unlock.py <sha256-of-tampered.txt>
challenges.scenario: A wire-transfer instruction may have been altered in transit. A hash is a fingerprint of a file - change a single byte and the whole hash changes (the avalanche effect). Compare the two files with SHA-256 to prove whether one was tampered with and identify the altered field.
challenges.objective: Prove the files differ with SHA-256, identify the change, and unlock the flag.

steps.title: Hash both files
steps.desc: The two SHA-256 values will not match.

steps.title: Find exactly what changed
steps.desc: A single field (the amount) was altered.

steps.title: Unlock the flag
steps.desc: Feed the SHA-256 of the tampered file to the unlocker.
